messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kofi had always been drawn to high-stress jobs, but nothing could have prepared him for the day a massive earthquake struck his hometown. As a bomb disposal technician, he was part of the emergency response team that rushed to the scene. The sounds of crumbling buildings and screams still echoed in his mind - loud noises that now made him jump at any moment. Shouting, too, transported him back to those chaotic hours, when every second counted and lives hung in the balance. Unpredictable situations, which had once been a thrilling aspect of his work, now filled him with dread. In the months following the disaster, Kofi found himself struggling to cope with these triggers. He began to eat excessively, using food as a distraction from the anxiety that gripped him. Avoiding anything stressful became second nature - he would turn down invitations to social events or decline tasks at work if they seemed too taxing. Keeping his mind occupied all the time was another tactic; he'd spend hours watching TV or scrolling through his phone to prevent any quiet moments where memories might creep in. But despite these efforts, Kofi's body continued to react as if it were still in danger. False alarms went off constantly - a sudden noise would make him leap out of bed, ready to respond to an emergency that wasn't there. Flashbacks hit without warning, and he'd find himself reliving the earthquake, his heart racing as if it were happening all over again. When these episodes passed, Kofi was left shaken, wondering why his mind couldn't shake off the feeling of being constantly on edge. The memories themselves remained fragmented - Kofi would push them away before they became too vivid, afraid of what he might recall. But when he did remember snippets, intense rage would flood through him. It made no sense to his rational mind, but the emotions lingered long after the memories faded. These incomplete recollections haunted him, leaving more questions than answers. As time passed, Kofi's maladaptive strategies only intensified the cycle of threat and memory. Eating excessively led to guilt and self-doubt, which in turn made him more prone to false alarms and flashbacks. Avoiding stressors meant missing out on essential tasks at work, further eroding his sense of control. Keeping his mind occupied all the time left no space for reflection or processing - memories continued to simmer just below the surface, waiting to boil over. Kofi's wife noticed the changes in him, but he pushed her away whenever she tried to talk about it. He was certain that he could handle this on his own, that seeking help would mean admitting weakness. Yet as the months turned into years, Kofi realized he couldn't keep living like this - constantly on edge, trapped in a cycle of fear and avoidance. It was then that he finally sought out professional help, hoping to break free from the hold of those haunting memories and find some semblance of peace. What brought him to therapy was the realization that his work as a bomb disposal technician had become unsustainable - every mission now felt like a threat to his own life. He couldn't shake the feeling that he was one wrong move away from disaster, that his body would always react before his mind could catch up. As Kofi sat in the therapist's office, he knew it wouldn't be easy to confront these demons, but he was ready to try - for himself, and for those around him who deserved a husband, father, and friend who wasn't constantly haunted by the ghosts of that fateful day.
